title: Chosen, not born
hookLine: the people choose one to govern them: a gentle satire of caste origins

cards: After the savory earth, the Agganna Sutta moves on: a kind of fungus, then a creeper, then rice that grows wild and ripens again overnight. Then someone gets lazy. Why go out twice a day?
I'll bring in enough for two meals. Others copy him, gathering for two days, then four, then eight. Soon the rice stops regrowing.
So they divide the land into fields, with boundaries. And one being, greedy again, guards his own plot and takes from someone else's. He's caught.
He promises not to do it again. He does it again.

teach.h: THEY GATHER AND TALK IT OVER.
teach.b: Theft appears, then blame, then lying, then punishment with sticks. So the beings gather and talk it over.
What if we picked one of us, someone who'd be angry when anger is right, blame what deserves blame, and banish who deserves banishing? We'd each give that person a share of rice.
They choose the best-looking, most pleasant, most capable among them. Chosen by agreement: not born to it, not sent down from heaven. Then the sutta gives each title a punning origin.
He's called Mahasammata, the great elect, because the people chose him. Khattiya, a noble, because he's lord of the fields. Raja, a king, because he delights people by doing what's right.

Then the brahmins: those who put away bad things, says the text. Some went to the forest to meditate. Others couldn't manage meditation, settled near villages compiling books, and were called non-meditators.

These derivations are wordplay, not dictionary etymology, and some scholars read them as deliberate satire. The wordplay is gentle, aimed at a claim about birth, not at anyone's faith. The point lands at the end.
People from any of the four classes can act badly, and people from any class can act well and be freed.
And the Buddha closes by quoting a verse he agrees with: the noble is best among those who care about clan, but one with knowledge and good conduct is best among gods and humans.

how: Buddhist teachers often cite the Agganna Sutta when they teach that a person's worth comes from conduct, not birth, and the sutta itself says someone from any of the four classes can go forth.

games.q: theft and fighting have started among the first people. what do they do in the story?
o: they gather and choose one capable person to govern, paid in rice.
they wait for a god to send a king.
games.why: they choose the most capable among them, the great elect, and each give him a share of rice.

practice: Think of someone who leads fairly: a manager, a coach, a teacher, an elected official you respect, the person who keeps your family or your team together.
Picture them doing the ordinary job well, settling a quarrel, sharing out the work, and let some gratitude come up for them. They weren't born to that; someone trusted them with it.

wordCard.voice: Chosen. In DN 27 the first ruler is chosen by the people, the great elect, and the old class titles are told with a wink. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali Mahasammata: the great elect, the first ruler chosen by the people in DN 27.

carryVoice: Your line: freed by what you do. Not by where you were born. That's day five hundred sixty-one.
